Introduction to Prevent

Prevent is part of the UK government’s Counter-terrorism strategy (CONTEST) 2023, which aims to stop people from becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism. The objectives of Prevent are to:

tackle the ideological causes of terrorism

intervene early to support people who may be susceptible to radicalisation

enable people who have already been engaged in terrorism to disengage and rehabilitate

Radicalisation is the process of a person legitimising support for, or use of, terrorist violence.

As a professional working in a mental health service, Prevent sits alongside your safeguarding responsibilities to your patients and the public.

Prevent works as follows:

If a professional within a mental health service has concerns about someone who may be susceptible to radicalisation, they should consider making a referral to Prevent.

Referrals are assessed by the police and, where appropriate, progressed to a multi-agency Channel panel.

Channel panels determine whether referred cases should be accepted into Channel and then discuss these cases to decide whether intervention is necessary, and if so, what type of intervention - see ‘The Channel process’ section below for more details. Often, mental health services have representatives who sit on these panels, alongside representatives from other sectors such as wider healthcare services, the police and education.

Channel panels may request additional information to support their discussions. You should share appropriate information when requested.

Channel panels may suggest a package of support to those who have been referred. Accepting the support offered is voluntary. This support may address areas such as:

employment

education

mental health

extremism-specific intervention support

Prevent operates mainly in the non-criminal space, focusing on preventing radicalisation before any offence occurs, although it does support people who may already have offending histories. Prevent runs alongside other well established safeguarding processes in place to protect both the person and the wider public.

This guidance expands on all the above, but for further information, including about statutory duties, see the Prevent duty guidance for specified authorities in England and Wales.

Your role

All staff

As a professional in a mental health service, engaging with Prevent sits alongside your safeguarding responsibilities towards your patients and the public.

You should therefore know what to do in circumstances where you might become concerned someone may be at risk of becoming radicalised. This includes:

making yourself familiar with the basic principles of the referral process

assessing each situation on a case-by-case basis

keeping up to date with your Prevent training

knowing who your organisation’s Prevent lead is

Your Prevent lead is likely to be part of your safeguarding team and should be your main point of contact on all things related to Prevent.

For further information about Prevent for all healthcare staff, see the Prevent duty: guidance for healthcare professionals.

Prevent leads

As the Prevent lead within your organisation, your role is to champion Prevent. Your main roles are to:

act as your organisation’s main Prevent contact, collaborating with staff to assess and support referrals

act as the main liaison with the police, Channel panels and other local agencies involved in Prevent

ensure your organisation has a Prevent policy outlining roles and expectations. At a minimum, it should include details on how to contact you and signpost required training and the national referral form, which you can download from the Get help for radicalisation concerns guidance page

provide quarterly updates to your organisation’s board and regular updates to your Channel panel chair

For full details of your role as a staff member or Prevent lead, read the rest of this guidance (including the accompanying ‘Your role under Prevent’ summaries) and see Prevent duty: core standards for healthcare commissioners and providers.

The NHS Prevent training and competencies framework covers training and competency requirements for different staff groups.

When you should consider making a referral

One rule always applies: if there is a risk of immediate harm to the person, yourself or others, contact 999 without delay.

You should be aware that there is no set criteria to determine when to make a referral. Radicalisation can take many different forms, and anyone, regardless of background, can be susceptible. A referral should be made if there is concern that a person may be at risk of becoming a terrorist or supporting terrorism.

Each person should be considered on a case-by-case basis using guidance and your professional judgement. Like any safeguarding mechanism, it is far better to receive a referral that turns out not to be of concern than for someone who genuinely needs support to be missed.

You should be aware of signs that someone may be susceptible to radicalisation. Susceptibility to radicalisation often develops through the interaction of multiple influences, including upbringing, environment, life experiences and social relationships, among others.

You should not regard a referral as being unfair to your patients or a breach of confidentiality. As with all other aspects of safeguarding, the intended outcome is to protect people from harm.

When assessing the potential susceptibility of someone and whether you should refer or not, consider the Notice, check, share framework.

Notice, check, share

Notice - be alert to signs of concern or changes in behaviour

There are many things that could be potential warning signs or reasons to be concerned, such as:

recent change in behaviour, such as spending time with groups who may be involved in concerning behaviour

increased online activity, such as engagement with extremist or hateful content, or material promoting or glorifying violence

It is part of your role to ensure that your organisation is represented on every Channel panel you are requested to be part of. Each local authority operates its own panel and, depending on the geographical boundaries of your organisation, you may need to engage with more than one panel. If you cannot attend all relevant panels personally, you must appoint a suitable representative to attend on behalf of the organisation.

For certain cases, it may be appropriate for a colleague with greater knowledge or direct involvement to attend the Channel panel meeting. Co-ordinate this where possible and ensure they are able to participate effectively.

Before each Channel panel meeting, you may be asked to sign a confidentiality agreement. All information shared is strictly protected and must not be disclosed outside the meeting unless there is a lawful and justified reason to do so.

Refer to the ‘Information sharing’ section below for further detail.

During a Channel panel meeting

The Channel panel meets to discuss each case, considering:

different perspectives

level of risk

types of support that may be appropriate

It is part of your role to ensure that mental health expertise feeds into this process, providing insights that other agencies may not be able to offer. If you do not have the relevant expertise yourself, it is part of your role to make sure that more appropriate colleagues are able to attend or contribute in some other meaningful way.

For adopted cases, a support plan will be developed based on the panel’s discussion. This may or may not include actions pertaining to mental health services. The exact support provided will vary and is tailored to the person. However, it generally falls into one of 3 broad categories:

Conceptual: specialist support can also be provided by an intervention provider. This is a trained professional with expertise in ideological drivers, extremist narratives and how to counter them. Typically, the intervention provider works with the person on a one-to-one basis, helping them to explore and process their thoughts in relation to extremism.

Practical: training to help improve skills, behaviour or knowledge, such as employment support.

Material: usually one-off material or financial support, such as transport costs to attend a course, or even re-housing.

Your support may include:

assisting panel members to understand mental health needs and how these may or may not contribute to the risk of radicalisation

assisting with formulating needs and wider multi-agency support requirements

providing intervention or support for co-occurring mental health needs

supporting referrals into relevant neurodevelopmental needs pathways

providing social prescribing options to reduce isolation and promote inclusion

supporting access to education pathways (such as further study, apprenticeships or training) to ensure meaningful routine and structure

After a Channel panel meeting

Ensure that all actions assigned to your organisation are completed promptly and recorded appropriately in the patient care record. This may include:

obtaining consent

arranging mental health assessments

facilitating treatment pathways

gathering supporting information

It is up to the person (or their parent or legal guardian if they are under 18 years old) if they accept support offered. You may be involved in supporting colleagues to provide the Channel panel with a signed agreement to show evidence that the person has given consent to receive support. Speak to your Channel panel chair or case officer about a consent form template.

If consent is not obtained, the case is closed to Channel. In these cases, consider other healthcare and safeguarding pathways.

Where referrals to mental health services or neurodevelopmental needs pathways are required, prioritise triage and assessment based on clinical need and risk. If service pressures limit this, clearly communicate your organisation’s capacity and any constraints to the Channel panel. If service pressures limit your capacity to fulfil actions assigned by Channel panels on a regular basis, share your concerns with your management and service commissioners.

Cases will continue to be monitored over time by the Channel panel. You may receive updates or be asked to provide updates ahead of future meetings. You should also begin preparing for the next Channel panel meeting where new people may be discussed.

Channel panel governance and reporting

Each Channel panel has its own local governance procedures covering processes, improvement and reporting. You should comply fully with these requirements, which may include providing regular updates or reports to the Channel panel.

Following their closure, all Channel cases are reviewed at 6-month and 12-month intervals. People are no longer part of the Prevent programme once the 12-month review is complete, and their data will be deleted by the Home Office 6 years later. For more details, see Channel and Prevent Multi-Agency Panel (PMAP): data privacy notices.

For more information on how Channel panels work:

see the ‘Prevent and the Channel process in the NHS: information sharing and governance’ guidance

ensure you have completed the Channel and PMAP training course

speak to your local authority Channel chair

Information sharing

Prevent relies on early and effective information sharing to protect people who may be susceptible to radicalisation.
